meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you come to a fork in the road, take it'?
meta.ogDescription: A signature Yogiism Berra genuinely adopted — yet the fork-in-the-road wordplay first appeared as a 1913 newspaper gag. The full provenance.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–2015 · Baseball Hall of Fame catcher, New York Yankees
answer.sourceLine: Widely and correctly associated with Berra, who embraced the line in The Yogi Book (1998) and made it a book title; but the wordplay appeared in a 1913 newspaper joke, the earliest tie to Berra is only 1988, and no source pins an original utterance by him.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: 1913, as a joke filler headed “Wise Directions”
The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!
1998 · embraced by Berra; later a 2001 book title

source.excerpt: “When you come to a fork in the road, take it.” “I will, if it is a silver one.”
trail: The seven-word wordplay first appears in a 1913 newspaper filler joke — “‘When you come to a fork in the road, take it.’ ‘I will, if it is a silver one.’” — per Quote Investigator, which cites the Fort Gibson New Era and Correctionville News of 31 July 1913.
The earliest link to Berra is only 1988; in his 1989 memoir he wasn’t even sure it was his — “I really don’t know about that one.”
By 1998 Berra had embraced it, printing it in The Yogi Book and later using it as a 2001 book title; the Yogi Berra Museum lists it among his Yogiisms.
Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed, noting the 1913 newspaper appearance.
source.cutTag: ↑ the 1913 gag had a second line — the popular version keeps only the setup
source.excerptNote: The oldest known form is a play on the two meanings of ‘fork’ (a road that splits vs. a table fork). Berra later gave it a literal explanation: he was directing Joe Garagiola to his Montclair, New Jersey home, where either branch of the fork led to the same house.

source.rightsNote: The phrase itself — a piece of anonymous 1913 wordplay — is old enough to be public domain. Berra’s books that reprint and explain it (The Yogi Book, 1998; When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!, 2001) remain under copyright as published works.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: About Yogi Berra
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Baseball Hall of Fame catcher & folk philosopher
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra was an 18-time All-Star catcher for the New York Yankees and a member of the Baseball Hall of Fame, part of ten World Series-winning teams. Off the field he became famous for “Yogiisms” — paradoxical one-liners like “It ain’t over till it’s over” and “Nobody goes there anymore, it’s too crowded.” He collected and embraced many of these sayings in his own books, even ones, like this fork-in-the-road line, that he hadn’t originally coined.

misattribution.heading: The catch
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual: Berra really did say it — but he didn’t invent the joke. The common assumption that the wordplay is original to him is what’s off.

items.scope: Commonly assumed to be coined by
items.why: The fork-in-the-road pun ran in newspapers as a stock joke in 1913 — twelve years before Berra was born (1925) — and wasn’t attached to his name until 1988. He popularized it; he didn’t originate it.
Asked about it, Berra said he wasn’t sure the saying was his — “I really don’t know about that one” — before later embracing it in 1998.

misattribution.truthLine: The truth: it’s a genuine Yogiism Berra adopted and made famous, but the wordplay is anonymous folk humor traceable to a 1913 newspaper joke, not something Berra coined.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The line works on three levels at once — as a literal traffic instruction, as a nonsense paradox (you can’t take a fork; you have to choose a branch), and as accidental wisdom about committing to a decision. That triple reading is exactly the shape of a great ‘Yogiism,’ and it’s why the quip outgrew its origins as an anonymous newspaper gag.

Berra gave it a straight-faced backstory: he was giving his friend Joe Garagiola directions to his home in Montclair, New Jersey, where the two branches of a fork in the road both looped back to his house — so it genuinely didn’t matter which you took.
context.pull: You can’t actually take a fork — and that’s the whole joke.
